lines.text: A jet built to break the sound barrier, without the big boom.
It's NASA's X-59, built by Lockheed Martin for quiet supersonic flight.
An airliner flies over land, but slower than sound.
A fighter jet goes faster, but its sonic boom rattles windows.
This one wants both.
In 1973, the U.S. banned civilian supersonic flight over land.
The secret is its shape.
On most supersonic jets, shock waves from the nose and wings merge into one big boom.
The X-59's long, thin nose is almost a third of its length.
Stretched out like that, the shock waves don't merge.
The engine sits on top, aiming its noise away from the ground.
So people below should hear a soft thump, if anything at all.
The cockpit sits almost halfway back, with no forward window.
The pilot looks ahead on a [4K](/fˈɔɹ kˈA/) screen, fed by cameras.
It's built to cruise at Mach 1.4, about 925 miles an hour.
NASA will fly it over U.S. towns and ask people what they heard.
That helps regulators set a noise limit for supersonic flight over land.
The hard part is proving it works in real air.
In 2003, an F-5E jet with a reshaped body made a quieter boom.
The X-59 first flew on October 28, 2025.
On June 5, 2026, it went supersonic for the first time.
The chase plane's booms drowned out any sound from the X-59.
By October, it was flying at Mach 1.4 and 55,000 feet.
Next, NASA measures the thump, then flies over towns to see if anyone hears it.
